title: The sign of the cross, again
hook: the smallest prayer you learned on day two
tomorrow: Mia's coming to Mass on Sunday. what will she see?

segments.voice: Yesterday: write the rule, and the line one page, plain enough to read on the run. The rule is done. Now a new stretch: looking back down the mountain, starting where it began.

Penalty kick. Before the run-up, the player touches forehead, chest, one shoulder, then the other, in about a second. The cameras catch it; nobody comments. It's the smallest prayer there is, and one of the first this path taught: in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. So, years later, a question with two good answers. Is it better quick and often, or slow and rare?
screen: `ONE SECOND BEFORE THE KICK.` → `THE FIRST PRAYER.` → `QUICK AND OFTEN, OR SLOW?`

segments.voice: The words come from the end of Matthew, where Jesus sends his friends out baptizing "in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost." The gesture has two Catholic voices pulling different ways. First, Tertullian, an early Christian writer from North Africa. He describes Christians tracing the sign on their foreheads at every turn: going in and out, putting on shoes, bathing, sitting down to eat, lighting the lamps. His case: make it often, and the whole ordinary day gets marked as God's, not only the big moments. A quick cross before a penalty kick fits him fine. Then the theologian Romano Guardini, who asks for the opposite: not a hurried, cramped flick, but a large, slow sign, forehead to breast, shoulder to shoulder, felt all the way. His case: made slowly, it gathers the whole person, thoughts, heart and body, under the cross, and it stays a prayer instead of becoming a twitch. One to tell a friend: in Tertullian's description, the sign is traced on the forehead, not drawn large from shoulder to shoulder. Both voices are Catholic. And both agree on the thing that matters: it's a prayer, a name spoken over a body.
screen: `IN THE NAME OF THE FATHER.` · `TERTULLIAN: AT EVERY TURN.` · `GUARDINI: SLOW AND LARGE.` · `EITHER WAY, A PRAYER.` · then, large: `WHERE IT BEGAN.`

segments.voice: Make the sign of the cross the slow way: hand to forehead, Father; down to the heart, Son; shoulder to shoulder, Holy Ghost. Give each touch a few seconds, and feel where your hand lands. If you don't pray, simply notice the shape the gesture draws over you.
The sign of the cross. A name traced over the body: quick at every turn, or slow and large, and a prayer either way.
screen: `THE SIGN OF THE CROSS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: where it began, a hand on the forehead and a name. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics make the sign of the cross at the start and end of prayers and of Mass, with holy water entering a church, and before meals, games, journeys or hard moments; some trace a small cross on the forehead, lips and heart before the Gospel.

chat.meaning: The sign speaks the name from Matthew 28 over the body. Quick or slow, Catholic voices agree it's a prayer, not a charm.
